title: Strict mode
subtitle: strict bundle, null checks, implicit any, class init

cards.front: What topics does unpacking strict assume?
cards.meaning: unknown vs any, narrowing, and Nest class patterns for definite assignment — those are how you live with the flags in real code.

cards.front: Is strict: true one compiler check?
cards.meaning: No. It is a shortcut that turns on a bundle of individual flags: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictPropertyInitialization, useUnknownInCatchVariables, alwaysStrict, noImplicitThis, and strictBindCallApply. Interviews want the bundle named, the important ones unpacked, and which matter most in production.

cards.front: Since when is catch-as-unknown part of strict?
cards.meaning: TS 4.4+ includes useUnknownInCatchVariables in the strict bundle, so catch (e) is e: unknown under modern strict.

cards.front: Can you turn one flag off under strict: true?
cards.meaning: Yes — you can enable strict and set an individual flag false while migrating (e.g. "strictNullChecks": false under "strict": true). Possible, but discouraged long-term.

cards.front: Which strict flag matters most, and what is second?
cards.meaning: strictNullChecks has the biggest real-world impact — without it null/undefined are silently assignable everywhere, defeating protection against null-reference crashes. noImplicitAny is a close second — it stops untyped parameters from becoming implicit any and disabling checking.

cards.front: What does strictNullChecks do?
cards.meaning: null and undefined are only assignable where the type allows them. Without it, they are assignable to almost every type, so string secretly means string | null | undefined in practice and the type system stops protecting you from reading a property of null/undefined.

cards.front: getLength(null) without strictNullChecks — compile or crash?
cards.meaning: It compiles and crashes at runtime. With strictNullChecks, null is not assignable to string.
cards.example: function getLength(s: string) { return s.length; } getLength(null); // compiles without the flag, errors with it

cards.front: How do you accept null under strictNullChecks?
cards.meaning: Type the parameter as string | null (or undefined as needed) and narrow before use. After if (s === null) return 0, s.length is narrowed to string.
cards.example: function getLengthSafe(s: string | null) { if (s === null) return 0; return s.length; }

cards.front: What must APIs do once strictNullChecks is on?
cards.meaning: They must say string | null when null is possible. You narrow before use (if, ??, optional chaining with care). This is why Nest/React code under strict is full of | null, guards, and definite assignment — modeling reality, not ceremony.

cards.front: Do optional properties involve undefined under strict null checks?
cards.meaning: Yes. prop?: T already involves undefined under strictNullChecks, so you treat missing and undefined as part of the type, not as a secret extra.

cards.front: What happens to function log(x) under noImplicitAny?
cards.meaning: Error: parameter 'x' implicitly has an 'any' type. With the flag off, x is implicitly any and checking is largely off for x. With it on, you annotate (or rely on context typing) so any is an explicit choice.
cards.example: function log(x) {} // error with noImplicitAny; function log(x: string) {} // ok

cards.front: Why does noImplicitAny matter beyond one parameter?
cards.meaning: any infects call sites. One untyped callback parameter can disable checking through a whole chain. The flag forces annotations or inference from context so any is not a silent default.

cards.front: Does noImplicitAny require annotating .map callbacks?
cards.meaning: No. Context typing still works: .map((n) => n + 1) on number[] can infer n without an annotation.

cards.front: Does strict or noImplicitAny ban all any?
cards.meaning: No. Explicit any is still allowed. noImplicitAny blocks inferred any on untyped parameters and similar holes, not every intentional any annotation — use those sparingly.

cards.front: Is (value: string) => void assignable to (value: string | number) => void under strictFunctionTypes?
cards.meaning: No. Handler may call with a number, so assigning stringOnly is an error. The flag compares function types more strictly, especially parameter positions (contravariance).
cards.example: type Handler = (value: string | number) => void; const stringOnly = (value: string) => {}; // error assigning stringOnly to Handler

cards.front: Why isn’t a Dog-only callback safe where an Animal callback is required?
cards.meaning: A function that accepts only Dog is not safely usable where a function that accepts Animal is required — the caller might pass a Cat. You do not need full variance theory: a narrower-parameter function is not a subtype of a wider-parameter function type.

cards.front: Were object methods always checked as strictly as function types?
cards.meaning: Methods on objects historically had looser (bivariant) checking in some cases. The flag’s day-to-day interview point: callback parameter types are not “anything goes”; unsafe assignments that used to slip through get caught.

cards.front: What does strictPropertyInitialization require?
cards.meaning: Class fields must be initialized in the declaration or constructor (or be optional / | undefined), unless you use a definite assignment assertion. Uninitialized private users: User[] is an error.
cards.example: class UserService { private users: User[]; constructor(private readonly repo: UserRepository) {} } // users error; repo param property is fine

cards.front: Do constructor parameter properties satisfy strictPropertyInitialization?
cards.meaning: Yes. constructor(private readonly repo: UserRepository) {} parameter properties are initialized — they are fine under the flag.

cards.front: How do you fix uninitialized Nest class fields under this flag?
cards.meaning: Give a default (private users: User[] = []), use definite assignment sparingly (private users!: User[]), or initialize via a constructor parameter property for DI.
cards.example: private users: User[] = [];  // or users!;  // or constructor(private readonly repo: UserRepository) {}

cards.front: When is private users!: User[] acceptable?
cards.meaning: Only when something else definitely assigns before read (framework DI, ngOnInit-style lifecycle you control). Abuse of ! reintroduces null crashes under a lie to the compiler. Do not spam ! on every Nest property instead of defaults or constructor init.

cards.front: What type is catch (e) under useUnknownInCatchVariables?
cards.meaning: e: unknown, not e: any (and that is the case under strict in modern TS). You must narrow, use instanceof Error, or a type guard before use — the same discipline as preferring unknown over any for untrusted values.
cards.example: try { await doWork(); } catch (e) { /* e: unknown */ }

cards.front: What does alwaysStrict do?
cards.meaning: Emit and parse with JavaScript strict mode ("use strict"). It catches sloppy-mode footguns such as accidental globals at the runtime-semantics level. Less “TS type” than “JS mode,” but it is part of the bundle.

cards.front: Is TypeScript strict the same as JS "use strict"?
cards.meaning: No. TypeScript strict is the type-check bundle. JS "use strict" is runtime language mode. They are related via alwaysStrict in the bundle, not identical — do not treat strictNullChecks as the same thing as "use strict".

cards.front: What does noImplicitThis catch?
cards.meaning: If this is not typed by a class, interface, or this parameter, TypeScript errors instead of treating this as any — e.g. an extracted function logging this.n.
cards.example: function orphan() { console.log(this.n); } // error: this is implicitly any

cards.front: What does strictBindCallApply check?
cards.meaning: bind / call / apply must match the function’s parameter types instead of accepting anything. greet.call(undefined, 123) is an error if greet expects a string.
cards.example: function greet(name: string) {} greet.call(undefined, 123); // error under the flag

cards.front: What does each strict flag buy you, in one line?
cards.meaning: strictNullChecks turns null crashes into type errors; noImplicitAny closes silent any holes; strictPropertyInitialization catches half-built class instances; useUnknownInCatchVariables means catch is not a free any; strictFunctionTypes catches unsafe callback assignment; noImplicitThis means floating this is not any; strictBindCallApply checks call/apply args; alwaysStrict emits/parses JS strict mode.

cards.front: Migrating a non-strict app — fix which flags first?
cards.meaning: Turn on strict, then fix strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny first — largest bug surface — before sweating the lower-profile flags.

cards.front: Why is turning off strictNullChecks “to ship faster” a bad trade?
cards.meaning: You lose most of TypeScript’s value: null and undefined become silently assignable everywhere again, which is the crash class the flag exists to catch.

cards.front: Does optional chaining replace modeling | null in APIs?
cards.meaning: No. Optional chaining is a tool after types tell the truth. You still declare string | null when null is possible, then narrow (if, ??, optional chaining with care).

cards.front: How does strictNullChecks connect to narrowing?
cards.meaning: It forces unions with null plus narrowing. Optional chaining and ?? are tools you use after the types actually admit null/undefined.

cards.front: How do noImplicitAny and useUnknownInCatchVariables connect to unknown vs any?
cards.meaning: Both enforce unknown-vs-any discipline: no silent any on parameters, and catch is unknown until you narrow — not a free any.

cards.front: How does strictPropertyInitialization show up in Nest?
cards.meaning: Via DI parameter properties, defaults like = [], and sparing use of definite assignment ! when the framework assigns the field.

cards.front: Where does strictFunctionTypes show up in React?
cards.meaning: Callback props and event handlers: a narrower-parameter function is not safely assignable where a wider-parameter callback is required.
